title: Codex Masters Class
description: A full Codex apprenticeship: prompt craft, refactoring, tests, debugging, architecture sketches, and shipping features with AI pair programming.

lessons.title: Codex Mindset: AI as a Junior Pair

introduction.text: Treat Codex like a fast junior engineer who needs clear specs. You own architecture, correctness, and taste. Codex drafts code; you review diffs, demand tests, and reject vague work. This mindset prevents blind copy-paste and builds a reusable prompting habit: goal → context → constraints → acceptance checks.

lessons.title: Prompt Anatomy for Code Generation

introduction.text: High-yield Codex prompts name the language, runtime, inputs/outputs, error behavior, and style rules. Add a minimal example or signature. Ask for a short plan before code when the task spans multiple files. Prefer “edit this function” over “rewrite the app.”

lessons.title: Explain, Navigate, and Document Codebases

introduction.text: Use Codex to map unfamiliar code: module purpose, call graphs, risky areas, and “how do I change X safely?” Ask for diagrams in Mermaid or bullet call chains. Demand citations as file paths and function names so you can verify.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify the explanation against real code

questions.question: A call chain summary helps you:
options: See how data flows through functions
questions.correctAnswer: See how data flows through functions

lessons.title: Refactoring and Code Health with Codex

introduction.text: Refactor in thin slices: extract function, rename for clarity, reduce nesting, then re-run tests. Tell Codex the invariant that must not change. Ask for a before/after complexity note and a regression checklist. Never mix feature work with large refactors in one prompt.

questions.question: Thin-slice refactors are safer because:
options: Each change is easier to review and revert
questions.correctAnswer: Each change is easier to review and revert

questions.question: An invariant is:
options: A behavior that must stay true
questions.correctAnswer: A behavior that must stay true

questions.question: A regression checklist should cover:
options: Happy path and edge cases you care about
questions.correctAnswer: Happy path and edge cases you care about

questions.question: Before refactoring, ensure you have:
options: A way to verify behavior (tests or cases)
questions.correctAnswer: A way to verify behavior (tests or cases)

questions.question: Asking for a diff-sized change means:

questions.correctAnswer: Understand why the change is better

lessons.title: Tests, Property Checks, and Fixtures

introduction.text: Have Codex propose test cases from the spec first, then implement. Cover happy path, boundaries, and failure modes. Prefer deterministic fixtures. Ask for table-driven tests when many inputs share structure. Use failing tests to drive fixes.

questions.question: Generating cases before code helps you:
Boundary tests target:
options: Limits like empty, max, zero, null
questions.correctAnswer: Limits like empty, max, zero, null

questions.question: Table-driven tests are good when:
options: Many inputs share the same assertion shape
questions.correctAnswer: Many inputs share the same assertion shape

questions.question: A failing test first is useful to:
options: Prove the bug and guide the fix
questions.correctAnswer: Prove the bug and guide the fix

questions.correctAnswer: Signal, not a substitute for thoughtful cases

lessons.title: Debugging Loops with Codex

introduction.text: Feed Codex the error, stack, relevant snippet, and what you already tried. Ask for ranked hypotheses, then a minimal experiment. Avoid dumping the whole repo. After a fix, request a regression test and a one-line root-cause summary for your notes.

options: Test the most likely causes first
questions.correctAnswer: Test the most likely causes first
